passages.t: A report, and a man sitting in horror
passages.happening:
Some months after Ezra's arrival, the leaders come to him with a report. “The people of Israel, including the priests and Levites, have not kept themselves separate from the surrounding peoples whose abominations are like those of the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites” (verse 1). “Indeed, the Israelites have taken some of their daughters as wives for themselves and their sons, so that the holy seed has been mixed with the people of the land. And the leaders and officials have taken the lead in this unfaithfulness!” (verse 2).

Ezra's response is not first to act but to grieve. ‘When I heard this report, I tore my tunic and cloak, pulled out some hair from my head and beard, and sat down in horror’ (verse 3). Those ‘who trembled at the words of the God of Israel’ (verse 4) gather around him, and he sits in horror until the evening offering.

Then he gets up, with his clothes still torn, falls on his knees, and spreads out his hands to the LORD his God (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Marriage between the returned community and the peoples around it was a real problem across this whole period. Nehemiah faced it again a generation later, and the prophet Malachi spoke against it in the same era. Marriage into the families of local leaders could bring land, trade and political ties, which may explain why verse 2 says that the leaders and officials led the way.

The list of peoples in verse 1 joins the old nations of Canaan named in the law to the Ammonites, Moabites and Egyptians. Most of those Canaanite peoples no longer existed as distinct peoples in the fifth century BC. The list is drawn on purpose from the law (Deuteronomy 7 and 23), and it says that the danger the law had warned of has come back. The peoples are described by their abominations, the law's word for the worship of other gods and the practices that went with it.

In the ancient world, marriage was not a private arrangement between two people. It joined two families, and it normally meant sharing the household's gods and worship. The law's ban on marrying into the peoples of Canaan gave a reason that was about faith: such marriages would turn Israel's children away from the LORD.

The holy seed in verse 2 means Israel, the people set apart for God. The word for unfaithfulness, maal, means breaking faith with someone owed loyalty. It is used of a wife's unfaithfulness, and of Israel's betrayal of God.

Tearing clothes, pulling out hair and sitting in silence were signs of mourning and horror, used at news of a death or a disaster. Ezra treats the report as a kind of death in the community. The evening offering was a customary hour of prayer, and kneeling with hands spread out toward heaven was the posture of earnest prayer, the posture of Solomon at the temple's dedication.
passages.later:
The law's warning was plain: ‘they will turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods’ (Deuteronomy 7:4). Solomon's story had shown what it meant. He loved many foreign women, ‘Yet Solomon clung to these women in love’ (1 Kings 11:2), and in his old age his heart turned to other gods.

The same problem returns in Nehemiah: ‘In those days I also saw Jews who had married women from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab’ (Nehemiah 13:23). And Malachi says, ‘For Judah has profaned the LORD’s beloved sanctuary by marrying the daughter of a foreign god’ (Malachi 2:11).

Isaiah had used the same phrase for the people who would survive judgment: ‘so the holy seed will be a stump in the land’ (Isaiah 6:13).
passages.hard:
Was Ezra's concern about foreign wives a form of ethnic exclusion?

Read today, the language of a holy seed mixed with the peoples of the land can sound racial. Some interpreters argue that Ezra and Nehemiah reflect a narrowing ethnic boundary in the community after the exile. They point out that other voices in the Bible, such as the book of Ruth and the prophecy in Isaiah 56 of foreigners joining themselves to the LORD, give a more open picture. On this reading, Scripture itself holds these views in tension.

Others argue that Ezra's concern is religious rather than racial. The peoples are described by their abominations, the law's word for idolatry and its practices. The law Ezra draws on, Deuteronomy 7, gives religious reasons. And in Ezra 6:21, outsiders who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the land to seek the LORD were welcomed to the Passover. Ruth herself is the example of a foreigner who joined Israel by taking Israel's God as her own. On this reading, the problem was not the wives' ancestry but households formed without any turning to the LORD, at a moment when a tiny community could easily be absorbed and lose its faith.

Both readings agree that the text is concerned with faithfulness to God, and both take seriously that what happened in chapter 10 was costly and painful.

Nothing in this chapter gives anyone today a warrant to break up a marriage or a family, or to look down on anyone because of where they come from.
passages.asks: Ezra's first response to bad news was grief and prayer, not a plan. Ask how you respond when you learn of wrong in your own community. And ask whether you tremble at God's words, as those who gathered around Ezra did, or at what other people will think.

passages.t: A prayer of shame, and a brief moment of grace
passages.happening:
Ezra prays. “O my God, I am ashamed and embarrassed to lift up my face to You, my God, because our iniquities are higher than our heads, and our guilt has reached the heavens” (verse 6).

He looks back over Israel's whole history. “From the days of our fathers to this day, our guilt has been great” (verse 7). Because of it, Israel's kings and priests were handed over to foreign kings, to the sword, to captivity and to shame, ‘as we are this day’ (verse 7).

“But now, for a brief moment, grace has come from the LORD our God to preserve for us a remnant and to give us a stake in His holy place. Even in our bondage, our God has given us new life and light to our eyes” (verse 8). ‘Though we are slaves, our God has not forsaken us in our bondage’ (verse 9). He has given them favor with the kings of Persia, new life to rebuild the house of God, and ‘a wall of protection in Judah and Jerusalem’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Ezra's prayer is one of the great prayers of confession in the Old Testament, beside Nehemiah 1 and 9 and Daniel 9. It moves in steps: from shame (verse 6), to history (verse 7), to present grace (verses 8-9), to present sin (verses 10-12), and at last to an admission that the people have no defense (verses 13-15).

Listen to the pronouns. The report spoke of the people and the leaders. Ezra's prayer speaks of the guilt as shared, his own and the people's together. He had no part in the marriages, yet he confesses as one of the guilty community. He does not point at others from outside.

The pictures are vivid. Guilt piled higher than their heads and reaching the heavens. A stake in God's holy place, like a tent peg driven into the ground: a fragile but real hold on the land and on God's presence. A wall of protection, given through the favor of the kings of Persia (verse 9).

The word for remnant here, peletah, means those who escaped. It keeps before the reader how narrowly the people had been spared. And Ezra does not pretend that the return has made them free. They are still slaves, subjects of a foreign king. The grace is real, and it is brief.
passages.later: Other prayers after the exile say the same. Daniel prays, ‘we have sinned and done wrong. We have acted wickedly and rebelled’ (Daniel 9:5). And in Nehemiah the people pray, ‘So here we are today as slaves in the land You gave our fathers to enjoy its fruit and goodness’ (Nehemiah 9:36).
passages.asks: Ezra counted himself among the guilty, though he had not done what they had done. Ask whether you pray for your church and your people as one of them, or as someone standing apart. And ask where, in a hard season, you have been given a brief moment of grace.

passages.happening:
“And now, our God, what can we say after this? For we have forsaken the commandments” (verse 10). Ezra recalls the law's words about a land ‘polluted by the impurity of its peoples’ (verse 11), and its command not to give daughters to their sons or take their daughters for Israel's sons (verse 12).

After all that has come upon them, he says, and though God has punished them less than their iniquities deserve and left them a remnant (verse 13), ‘shall we again break Your commandments and intermarry with the peoples who commit these abominations?’ (verse 14). Would God not then be so angry as to leave no remnant at all?

The prayer ends: “O LORD, God of Israel, You are righteous! For we remain this day as a remnant. Here we are before You in our guilt, though because of it no one can stand before You” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Ezra prays in the words of the law. His picture of the land polluted by the practices of its peoples comes from the law of Moses, from Leviticus 18, and his words about daughters and sons come from Deuteronomy 7.

His fear is that the very sin that led to the exile has come back. The people had been spared, a remnant brought home, and now they were walking the same road again. Behind the fear stands the memory of Solomon and of the kings who followed other gods.

The prayer ends without a request. Ezra does not ask God to forgive, or to fix it. He says that God is righteous, and that the people stand before him with nothing to plead. Repentance here begins in grief over sin, before it moves to action. What the community does next is told in chapter 10.
passages.later:
The law had warned of the land itself: ‘Even the land has become defiled, so I am punishing it for its sin’ (Leviticus 18:25).

And a psalm asks the question Ezra's prayer ends on: ‘If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand?’ (Psalm 130:3).
passages.asks: Ezra's prayer asks for nothing. Ask whether you have ever come to God with nothing to plead but his righteousness and mercy. And ask what it would mean to confess honestly, without excuses, before you decide what to do.
